t.2.23.1: Having saluted Kausalyā, Rāma, for whom his mother had performed the rites invoking blessings, and who stood firm on the most righteous path, set out for the forest.
t.2.23.3: And Vaidehī too, poor lady, had heard nothing of all that; in her heart there was only that consecration of him as heir apparent.
t.2.23.2: Illuminating the royal highway thronged with people, the king's son, by his abundance of virtues, seemed to stir the very hearts of the folk.
t.2.23.4: Having performed the rites to the gods, she, grateful and glad at heart, well versed in the duties of kings, was waiting for the prince.
t.2.23.5: Then Rāma entered his own richly adorned residence, filled with joyful people, his face lowered somewhat out of modesty.
t.2.23.6: Then Sītā, springing up and trembling, beheld her husband, scorched with grief, his senses thrown into turmoil by anxiety.
t.2.23.7: Seeing him pale-faced, sweating and unable to bear his distress, she, tormented with grief, said: "What is this now, my lord?"
t.2.23.9: Your lovely face does not shine, shaded by the hundred-ribbed parasol white as the foam of water.
t.2.23.8: O Rāghava, do the wise brāhmaṇas not declare that today the glorious Puṣya, the asterism of Bṛhaspati, is in conjunction? Why, then, are you so downcast?
t.2.23.10: Your face, with eyes like hundred-petalled lotuses, is not being fanned by the two foremost fans, brilliant as the moon and the swan.
t.2.23.11: O bull among men, the eloquent bards, the sūtas and the māgadhas, who joyfully praise you with auspicious songs, are not to be seen today.
t.2.23.12: Those brāhmaṇas, masters of the Vedas, did not, according to the prescribed rite, place honey and curds upon the head of the one whose head was to be anointed.
t.2.23.13: Neither all the subjects, nor the adorned heads of the guilds, nor likewise the people of the city and the countryside wish to follow you.
t.2.23.14: Why does the chief festive chariot, yoked with four swift horses adorned with gold, not go before you?
t.2.23.15: Nor, O hero, is your splendid elephant, honoured for its auspicious marks and shining like a dark cloud or a mountain, seen going before you on your departure.
t.2.23.16: Nor do I see, O handsome one, your auspicious seat adorned with gold, preceded by heroes, carried before you as you come.
t.2.23.17: When the consecration is all prepared, what is this in you now? An unusual pallor is seen on your face, and no joy is to be seen.
t.2.23.18: To her, lamenting thus, Raghunandana spoke: "Sītā, my revered father is banishing me to the forest."
t.2.23.20: Long ago my father, King Daśaratha, true to his promise, with a delighted heart granted two great boons to Kaikeyī.
t.2.23.19: O Jānakī, you who know dharma and live by dharma, sprung from a great and noble family, hear how, step by step, this has come upon me.
t.2.23.22: For fourteen years I must dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest, and my father has appointed Bharata to the office of heir apparent. So I, having set out for the desolate forest, have come to see you.
t.2.23.21: Today, when this consecration of mine, undertaken by the king, stood ready, that pact was pressed by her, and through dharma it carried the day.
t.2.23.23: In Bharata's presence I should never be praised by you, for men endowed with prosperity do not tolerate the praise of another. Therefore my virtues should not be spoken of by you before Bharata.
t.2.23.24: Nor will he ever support you with any special favor; only by being agreeable can one remain near him.
t.2.23.25: And I too, faithfully keeping that promise of my father, will go to the forest this very day; be steadfast, O noble-minded lady.
t.2.23.26: And when I have gone to the forest frequented by sages, O auspicious one, you, O sinless one, must remain devoted to vows and fasting.
t.2.23.27: Rising at daybreak and performing worship of the gods according to the prescribed rites, you should pay homage to Daśaratha, my father, the lord of men.
t.2.23.28: And my mother Kausalyā, aged and worn down by grief, deserves honor from you, placing righteousness foremost.
t.2.23.29: And those who remain, my other mothers, should always be honored by you, for in affection, love and care all my mothers are equal to me.
t.2.23.30: Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, who are dearer to me than my very life, should be regarded by you with special care, as equal to brothers and sons.
t.2.23.31: And nothing displeasing should ever be done to Bharata, for he is the king and the lord of both the land and the family.
t.2.23.32: For kings, when propitiated by good conduct and served with diligent efforts, become gracious; but in the opposite case they grow angry.
t.2.23.33: For kings abandon even their own sons born of their body when they do harm, and they embrace even common people who are capable.
t.2.23.34: I shall go to the great forest, my beloved, and you must remain right here, O lovely lady. You must carry out this word of mine in such a way that you give offense to no one.
